clinician.trajectory_summary: A 70-year-old male presented with refractory right-sided facial paralysis (House Brackmann VI) for 2 months, unresponsive to initial intravenous therapy. An MRI showed suggested recurrent cholesteatoma and facial nerve contrast enhancement and thickening, interpreted as neuritis, but no intracranial tumors. Surgical exploration of the right mastoid removed a small cholesteatoma, but it was not in contact with the facial nerve and was ruled out as the cause of the facial nerve paralysis. Facial nerve decompression was not performed due to long segment enhancement. A parotid biopsy was performed, which showed no signs of malignancy or inflammation. Subsequently, the main stem of the facial nerve was resected. Histological examination of the resected facial nerve confirmed infiltration by squamous cell carcinoma.
